title: Ancient Roman Temporal Clock
intro: This Roman temporal-hours model divides daylight into twelve seasonal hours and darkness into four night watches. The units vary in duration with season and latitude.
structure: Daylight uses Hour I through XII, starting at computed sunrise. Night uses Watch I through IV, starting at sunset. The optional fine display gives completed twelfths (unciae) of the current daylight hour, not modern minutes or seconds. Night watches have no fractional display.
example: For an illustrative 15-hour day, each temporal hour is 75 ordinary minutes. 37.5 minutes into the first hour is Hour I, VI twelfths. The nine-hour night divides into four watches of 135 minutes each.
history: Roman daylight horae were seasonal; the selected night convention uses four vigiliae. Other Roman historical contexts used different divisions, which are not all represented by this model.
model: Compute apparent solar phase and dawn/dusk from compact solar geometry using a 0.833-degree horizon correction. Select the day or wrapped night span, scale position into twelve or four parts and floor the period index. Fine daylight mode floors the fractional position times twelve, omitting a zero fraction. Labels are localised; scheduling searches for the next visible change.
limits: Requires valid latitude and longitude. If no solar crossing exists, display N/A rather than inventing a seasonal hour. The model is approximate, not a reconstruction of every historical Roman locality or observed water clock. The solar model assumes an idealised sea-level horizon and standard depression; local terrain and weather are not modelled.
